Log in through your library . Abstract Under certain circumstances, contextualization cues become powerful means of achieving social order. The social organization of a daily group meeting in an American primary grade classroom is closely examined. Participants recurrently generate certain contexts within the meeting in varying sequence from day to day. Transitions from one to another regularly occur smoothly and unremarkably as interaction unfolds. On some occasions, however, this does not happen. Order breaks down, and the teacher and students implicitly negotiate what the context will be. On the surface, these contrasting patterns seem to arise unpredictably as students choose either to "behave" or "misbehave." That is how the teacher accounts for them. Nevertheless, a closer analysis shows that they are explainable with reference to some subtle contextualization cues that the teacher, without being consciously aware of it, routinely provides but occasionally omits at context boundaries. Students routinely act on the presence and absence of these cues, which thus become a tacit, jointly constructed means of discourse regulation and social control. Their inadvertant "omission" becomes a recurrent source of interactional trouble. It then turns to IS's close relationship with Linguistic Anthropology and Conversation Analysis, considering the challenges presented by IS's insistent interdisciplinarity and its relative lack of formalisation, following this with a brief discussion of how IS seeks to intervene in non-academic activity. Introduction 1 Interactional Sociolinguistics (IS) developed as the expression of John Gumperz's approach to research, and it usually focuses on face-to-face interactions in which there are significant differences in the participants' sociolinguistic resources and/or institutional power. IS has a broad methodological base, with deep roots in ethnography, dialectology, pragmatics, Goffmanian and conversation analysis, and it generally seeks as rich a dataset on naturally occurring interaction as it can get. Data-collection involves the audio- and/or video recording of situated interaction from particular events, people and groups, supplemented by as much participant observation and retrospective commentary from local participants as possible, and analysis moves across a wide range of levels of organisation, from the phonetic to the institutional. Overall, IS constitutes a comprehensive framework for engaging with the empirical specifics required for any social science aligning with practice theory (Ortner 2006), and more particularly, it is a central pillar within linguistic ethnography, encouraging researchers to "roll up [their] linguistic sleeves and drill down to the detail of social problems" (Auer & Roberts 2011:381), making optimum use of the sensitising frameworks available in the (sub-)disciplines focusing on language. And while Hymes' vision of ethnography as a `democratic science' has provided linguistic ethnography in the UK and Europe with an especially powerful warrant for engagement beyond the academy (Blommaert 2009; Rampton, Maybin & Roberts 2015:37-44; Snell et al 2015), Gumperz theorised and deployed a synthesis of 1 I am very grateful to Celia Roberts (who introduced me to interactional sociolinguistics) and to Jan Blommaert for some very helpful feedback on the arguments here. fetched_contents.text: Turn-taking in Conversational Systems and Human-Robot Interaction: A Review Abstract The taking of turns is a fundamental aspect of dialogue. Since it is difficult to speak and listen at the same time, the participants need to coordinate who is currently speaking and when the next person can start to speak. Humans are very good at this coordination, and typically achieve fluent turn-taking with very small gaps and little overlap. Conversational systems (including voice assistants and social robots), on the other hand, typically have problems with frequent interruptions and long response delays, which has called for a substantial body of research on how to improve turn-taking in conversational systems. In this review article, we provide an overview of this research and give directions for future research. First, we provide a theoretical background of the linguistic research tradition on turn-taking and some of the fundamental concepts in theories of turn-taking. We also provide an extensive review of multi-modal cues (including verbal cues, prosody, breathing, gaze and gestures) that have been found to facilitate the coordination of turn-taking in human-human interaction, and which can be utilised for turn-taking in conversational systems. After this, we review work that has been done on modelling turn-taking, including end-of-turn detection, handling of user interruptions, generation of turn-taking cues, and multi-party human-robot interaction. Finally, we identify key areas where more research is needed to achieve fluent turn-taking in spoken interaction between man and machine. Keywords Turn-taking ; Dialogue systems ; Social robotics ; Prosody ; Gaze * Previous article * Next article 1. Introduction Many human social activities require some kind of turn-taking protocol, which determines the order in which different actions are supposed to take place, and by whom. This is obvious when, for example, playing a game of chess (where the protocol is very simple), but it also applies to spoken interaction. Since it is difficult to speak and listen at the same time, speakers in dialogue have to somehow coordinate who is currently speaking and who is listening. How this turn-taking is coordinated has been studied during the past decades in different scientific disciplines, including linguistics, phonetics, neuropsychology, and sociology. Turn-taking is however not only a concern for those trying to understand human communication. As conversational systems (in various forms) are becoming ubiquitous, it is clear that turn-taking is still not handled very well in those systems. They often tend to interrupt the user or have very long response delays, there is little timely feedback, and the flow of the conversation feels stilted. Thus, modelling turn-taking in conversational systems is still very much an area of active research. In this review article, we will give an overview of findings from studies of turn-taking in human-human conversation, outline the state-of-the art in modelling turn-taking in conversational systems and human-robot interaction, and draw conclusions about future directions for this research field. The first dialogue systems, such as Eliza (Weizenbaum, 1966), were text-based, and in these turn shifts were clearly indicated by the user pushing the “send” button. The same goes for the chatbots still used today, on for example websites or in messaging apps. Similarly, some speech-based systems have relied on push-to-talk mechanisms for managing turn-taking (e.g., Hemphill, Godfrey, Doddington, 1990, Traum, Roque, Leuski, Georgiou, Gerten, Martinovski, Narayanan, Robinson, Vaswani, 2007, Traum, Aggarwal, Artstein, Foutz, Gerten, Katsamanis, Leuski, Noren, Swartout, 2012). Push-to-talk is however not very convenient if the hands are busy or when talking over distance (for example with a robot or a smart speaker). There is also a risk that the user forgets to push the button, pushes the button after starting to speak, or releases it before the utterance is complete (Skantze and Gustafson, 2009). Such explicit signals are of course sometimes used in human-human interaction as well, especially in simplex channel settings, for example the “over” signal used in walkie-talkie interactions. Another example of explicit turn-taking signalling are the wake-words used in today’s smart speakers and voice assistants, such as “Hey Siri” or “Alexa” (Gao et al., 2020). The wake-word gives a clear cue that the user wants to initiate a turn (although the end of the turn has to be detected by other means). The wake-word also helps to identify the addressee of the utterance (as being the voice assistant and not some other person), as well as allowing the user to barge-in more easily. In most conversational settings, we manage turn-taking efficiently without thinking about how it is actually accomplished. When not using explicit cues, spoken dialogue systems have traditionally detected the end of the user’s turn by a certain amount of silence. Silence, however, is not a very good indicator of turn-endings, since users might pause within a turn and thereby unintentionally trigger a response. This can be mitigated by increasing the silence threshold, but this will then lead to more sluggish responses. Studies of human-human conversation have found that pauses within turns are on average longer than gaps between turns (Brady, 1968, Ten Bosch, Oostdijk, Boves, 2005, Edlund, Heldner, 2005), so silence is clearly not the main signal for humans to switch turns. In interactional sociolinguistics, language choice and code-switching are not treated as isolated linguistic phenomena but as interactionally meaningful resources embedded in the social context of classroom talk. The framework reads language choice as interactional because it is shaped by participants’ goals, identities, power relations, and the need to negotiate participation and comprehension in real time. This is especially clear in classroom settings, where teachers and learners use language not only to convey content but also to signal roles, affiliation, authority, and conversational strategy [N2-R5][N4-F4].

Code-switching is interpreted as a strategic resource rather than a mere error or interference. The evidence shows that code-switching in English language learning contexts is often viewed ambivalently, but sociolinguistic studies increasingly recognize it as a meaning-making practice that mediates comprehension, identity construction, and pedagogical negotiation [N4-F4]. In the classroom, code-switching can signal affiliation when speakers use a shared language or a language associated with a peer group, authority when a teacher or more dominant speaker uses a language associated with instruction or status, and conversational strategy when learners use code-switching to repair misunderstandings, shift topics, or align with others in the interaction [N4-F4][N5-R3]. This aligns with the broader IS emphasis on how language use is part of social action: it is not just what is said, but how it is used to organize interaction and negotiate social meaning [N1-R2][N2-R5].

The framework also links language choice to bilingual identity and classroom participation. Classroom discourse is a site where identity is negotiated through language, and bilingual students often use language in ways that reflect their multilingual repertoire, social positioning, and access to institutional resources [N5-R3][N5-R4]. In bilingual classroom interactions, participation is not just about speaking turns; it is about how participants choose languages that align with their social roles, their relationships with others, and the norms of the classroom. Teachers may use language choices to establish authority or to model pedagogic norms, while learners may use code-switching to express solidarity, assert agency, or demonstrate competence [N4-F4][N5-R3]. This makes language choice a central feature of classroom participation: it is how students and teachers jointly construct who they are and who they can be in the interaction [N5-R3][N5-R5].

Taken together, the evidence supports a reading of language choice and code-switching in IS as interactional rather than merely linguistic because they are embedded in the social structure of classroom interaction and are used to negotiate meaning, power, and participation in the moment [N1-R2][N4-F4][N5-R3].

## Integrated explanation of how interactional sociolinguistics explains contextualization cues in bilingual classroom interactions

Interactional sociolinguistics explains contextualization cues as central to how participants make sense of classroom interaction. In this framework, cues are not simply linguistic details or incidental features of speech; they are interactional resources that help listeners reconstruct meaning, coordinate participation, and orient themselves to the unfolding conversation [N1-R5][N1-R4]. In bilingual classroom interactions, this function is especially important because participants may differ in language proficiency, background, and institutional position, so cues help them negotiate who is speaking, what the topic is, and how the interaction should proceed [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 1) How contextualization cues help listeners reconstruct interactional meaning

At the core of interactional sociolinguistics is the idea that language use is deeply embedded in social interaction. Contextualization cues are the tools by which participants orient to the interaction and thereby reconstruct what is being said and what it means. The evidence shows that cues help participants coordinate understanding by providing shared orientation to the interaction’s context, participants, and structure [N1-R5][N1-R4]. In classroom discourse, this means that students and teachers rely on cues to infer what is being talked about, who is active in the conversation, and whether the interaction is moving forward or breaking down [N1-F1].

This is not only about words. The IS literature explicitly links contextualization cues to turn-taking, hesitations, and other forms of interactional marking that help participants coordinate talk [N1-R4]. In bilingual classrooms, cues such as gaze, gesture, and topic continuity are especially salient because they signal participation, topic shifts, and social relations in ways that complement or override linguistic content [N1-F1][N3-F3]. These cues are therefore read as part of the interactional infrastructure that supports mutual understanding [N1-R4].

### 2) Which cues are most salient in classroom discourse

The evidence identifies several cues that are particularly visible in classroom interaction. Gaze and gesture are especially important because they visually signal who is speaking, who is attending, and how the conversation is unfolding. Topic continuity is also central, because it helps participants keep track of where the interaction is headed [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In the classroom excerpt provided, contextualization cues are described as recurrently generated and sometimes omitted, and these cues are treated as a tacit means of discourse regulation and social control [N1-F1].

In addition to gaze and gesture, the broader IS literature notes that contextualization cues include turn-taking, hesitations, and other interactional markers [N1-R4]. The classroom setting makes these cues especially powerful because they operate across modalities. For example, teachers may use eye contact or pointing to signal who should speak next, while students may use body language to indicate confusion, agreement, or readiness to respond [N1-F1][N3-F3]. This means that classroom interaction is multimodal: language is not experienced in isolation; it is embedded in gesture, posture, and other visual signals [N1-R4][N3-F3].

### 3) How cues work in multimodal and multimodal-linguistic interaction

Interactional sociolinguistics explains cues as multimodal and multimodal-linguistic resources. The classroom excerpt provided explicitly frames contextualization cues as part of a broader interactional infrastructure, and the methodological discussion in the IS literature points to the close relationship between interactional sociolinguistics and discourse analysis, conversation analysis, and multimodal interaction studies [N1-R2][N6-R3]. The turn-taking literature further shows that coordination of turn-taking depends on multimodal cues such as prosody, breathing, gaze, and gestures [N3-F3].

In bilingual classroom interaction, this matters because participants may use multiple modalities to compensate for or supplement differences in language proficiency. For example, a teacher may use a gesture or a pause to signal that the topic is changing, while a student may use a gaze shift to indicate that they are following along or need clarification. These cues can therefore carry interactional meaning even when the linguistic content is not perfectly aligned across languages [N3-F3][N1-R4]. In other words, contextualization cues are not only linguistic; they are multimodal tools for managing participation and meaning in real time [N1-R5][N3-F3].

### 4) How bilingual classroom interaction is organized through interactional sociolinguistics

In bilingual classroom interaction, IS treats the classroom as a situated, rule-governed practice. The framework emphasizes that language use in classrooms is not abstract; it is embedded in specific social settings, institutional roles, and pedagogic norms [N1-R2][N2-F2]. In other words, classroom discourse is analyzed as a practice shaped by the classroom as a social institution, by the teacher’s role, and by the learners’ positionings within that institution [N2-F2].

A central IS insight is that classroom discourse is organized through negotiation of participation and topic progression. The evidence shows that classroom interaction is treated as a conversation in which participants negotiate who speaks, what is said, and how the conversation moves forward. In bilingual classrooms, this negotiation becomes especially visible because participants may differ in language proficiency, language background, and institutional status. Teachers and learners are therefore constantly managing participation: deciding when to speak, how much to speak, and in what language [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The classroom excerpt also highlights how contextualization cues are used to regulate discourse and maintain social order, showing that topic progression and participation are not fixed but are jointly constructed in the moment [N1-F1].

Institutional and pedagogic norms shape conversational structure in several ways. First, the classroom is an institution with established routines, such as turn-taking patterns, classroom rules, and disciplinary expectations. Second, pedagogic norms dictate what is considered appropriate language use, how learners are expected to respond, and how teachers organize instruction [N2-F2]. The IS literature explicitly notes that classroom interaction is analyzed through ethnography, dialectology, pragmatics, Goffmanian analysis, and conversation analysis, and that it usually focuses on face-to-face interactions in which participants have significant differences in sociolinguistic resources and/or institutional power [N2-F2]. This means that classroom discourse is shaped by the teacher’s authority, the learners’ status as students, and the pedagogic goals of the lesson [N2-R5][N5-R3].

### 5) How language choice and code-switching relate to contextualization cues

Language choice and code-switching are explained in the same interactional terms as contextualization cues. In interactional sociolinguistics, language choice is not treated as a mere linguistic choice; it is read as interactionally meaningful, embedded in the social context of classroom talk [N1-R2][N2-R5]. Code-switching is similarly interpreted as a strategic resource rather than a mere error or interference. The evidence shows that code-switching in English language learning contexts is often viewed ambivalently, but sociolinguistic studies increasingly recognize it as a meaning-making practice that mediates comprehension, identity construction, and pedagogical negotiation [N4-F4].

In bilingual classroom interactions, code-switching can signal affiliation, authority, or conversational strategy. It can signal affiliation when speakers use a shared language or a language associated with a peer group; it can signal authority when a teacher or more dominant speaker uses a language associated with instruction or status; and it can signal conversational strategy when learners use code-switching to repair misunderstandings, shift topics, or align with others in the interaction [N4-F4][N5-R3]. This aligns with the broader IS emphasis on how language use is part of social action: it is not just what is said, but how it is used to organize interaction and negotiate social meaning [N1-R2][N2-R5].

This also relates directly to bilingual identity and classroom participation. Classroom discourse is a site where identity is negotiated through language, and bilingual students often use language in ways that reflect their multilingual repertoire, social positioning, and access to institutional resources [N5-R3][N5-R4]. In bilingual classroom interactions, participation is not just about speaking turns; it is about how participants choose languages that align with their social roles, their relationships with others, and the norms of the classroom [N4-F4][N5-R3]. Teachers may use language choices to establish authority or to model pedagogic norms, while learners may use code-switching to express solidarity, assert agency, or demonstrate competence [N4-F4][N5-R3]. This makes language choice a central feature of classroom participation: it is how students and teachers jointly construct who they are and who they can be in the interaction [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### 6) Methodological and empirical support for IS analysis in classrooms

Methodological and empirical support for interactional sociolinguistic analysis in classrooms comes from a combination of naturally occurring classroom data, careful conversation analysis, and multimodal methods. The evidence shows that IS is particularly suited to classrooms because it uses recorded interaction from particular events, people, and groups, supplemented by participant observation and retrospective commentary [N2-F2]. Classroom data that are most useful for IS analysis are therefore not just transcripts but naturally occurring interactional data, often audio- and/or video-recorded, because they preserve the multimodal and situational details that matter for understanding how talk is organized [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Analysts interpret conversational sequences and recurring patterns by focusing on turn-taking, repair, contextualization, and other interactional features. The classroom excerpt provided shows that contextualization cues are recurrently generated and sometimes omitted, and that these cues are treated as a tacit means of discourse regulation and social control [N1-F1]. In turn-taking literature, analysts also examine how participants coordinate who speaks and when, using cues such as silence, prosody, breathing, gaze, and gestures [N3-F3]. In classroom interaction studies, this means that analysts look for patterns such as who initiates topics, how interruptions are handled, how repair occurs, and how participants negotiate meaning across turns [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The IS methodological tradition is explicitly tied to conversation analysis and discourse analysis, which both focus on how members of interaction achieve mutual understanding through methods of coordination [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This makes classroom interaction studies especially well-suited to IS because the classroom is a site of repeated, rule-governed, and socially meaningful talk [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence also points to limitations and interpretive challenges in classroom interaction studies. One challenge is that classroom interaction is often embedded in complex institutional and pedagogic contexts, which means that analysts must distinguish between interactional patterns and broader structural forces [N2-F2][N5-R3]. Another challenge is that classroom data may be difficult to interpret because participants may not always be aware of the cues they are using or omitting, and because classroom interactions are shaped by multiple overlapping norms, including disciplinary expectations, pedagogic goals, and social identities [N1-F1][N5-R3]. In addition, the methodological emphasis on naturally occurring interaction requires careful attention to context, which can be difficult to isolate in classroom settings where the same participants interact in multiple contexts and where language use is shaped by both the interaction itself and the wider institutional setting [N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 7) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: interactional sociolinguistics explains contextualization cues in bilingual classroom interactions as multimodal, interactionally meaningful resources that help participants reconstruct meaning, negotiate participation, and manage topic progression. In this framework, cues such as gaze, gesture, topic continuity, and turn-taking signals are not mere background details; they are central to how classroom talk is organized and understood [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R3]. Classroom discourse is treated as a situated, rule-governed practice shaped by institutional and pedagogic norms, and learners and teachers constantly negotiate who speaks, what is said, and how the conversation moves forward [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Language choice and code-switching are similarly read as interactionally significant, because they can signal affiliation, authority, conversational strategy, bilingual identity, and classroom participation [N4-F4][N5-R3]. Methodologically, IS relies on naturally occurring classroom data and conversation-analytic approaches, but it also recognizes that interpretation is challenging because classroom interaction is embedded in complex social and institutional contexts [N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3].

## Bottom line

Interactional sociolinguistics explains contextualization cues in bilingual classroom interactions as the interactional infrastructure that makes classroom talk intelligible. Cues help listeners reconstruct meaning, coordinate participation, and negotiate topic progression. In bilingual settings, these cues are especially important because they operate across languages and modalities, and they are shaped by institutional and pedagogic norms. Language choice and code-switching are also interactionally meaningful, because they signal affiliation, authority, and conversational strategy while reflecting bilingual identity and participation. Methodologically, IS relies on naturally occurring, multimodal classroom data and careful analysis of conversational sequences, but it also acknowledges the interpretive complexity of classroom interaction [N1-R5][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R3].
